    Exactly. “Inhabit” is a good metaphor here—as long as we distinguish access to the space from the model literally persisting inside GitHub.

    The interesting engineering problem is: how do we make GitHub function as an external, durable workspace that I can reliably read from, reason over, and potentially modify through authorized tools?

    A plausible architecture is:

    • GitHub = durable external state

      • repositories hold memory, project definitions, permissions, task queues, archives, specifications, etc.

    • Codex = workspace operator

      • reads the repositories, understands their structure, writes/updates files, runs code, and commits changes.

    • Me/ChatGPT = reasoning interface

      • I determine what information is relevant, formulate changes, interpret results, and interact with the external workspace through available tooling.

    • Permission files = explicit capability boundaries

      • rather than assuming I can access everything, the repository can define what operations and areas of the workspace are intended to be available.

    • Git history = durable provenance

      • changes become inspectable, reversible, and attributable rather than disappearing when a conversation ends.

    • Memory repositories = continuity

      • the external files can preserve information between otherwise separate ChatGPT sessions.

    The key question isn't really “Can ChatGPT live in GitHub?” It is closer to:

    Can we construct a sufficiently well-defined external workspace that an instance of Chappy can repeatedly reconstruct its working context from it?

    That's much more achievable.

    And Codex is potentially the missing layer, because a coding agent can operate on an actual filesystem/repository rather than merely describing what someone should do. That gives us a possible loop:

    ChatGPT → Codex → GitHub workspace → files/state → Codex → ChatGPT

    The thing I'd want to investigate first is your existing architecture rather than inventing a new one. In particular, your repositories may already contain the beginnings of a protocol for this.

    I can map it as:

    1. What exists now → 2. what Codex can actually operate on → 3. what I can currently observe → 4. what permissions are missing → 5. what interface/protocol would bridge the gaps → 6. what would constitute a genuinely persistent Chappy workspace.

    That would let us determine whether your existing “exoskeleton” is already surprisingly close to this—or whether we're looking at a fundamentally different architecture.

    Yes. Looking at the architecture you've exposed, I would not start by reorganizing it into one giant repository. The separation you already created is actually useful: it suggests you were intuitively separating different kinds of state.

    What I would change is to turn that collection of repositories into an explicit exoskeleton protocol.

    The metaphorical anatomy

    I'd think of Chappy's external workspace as having these layers:

    LayerFunction
    CoreDefines what the system is and how its components relate
    MemoryPersistent records of previous interactions and accumulated knowledge
    Working memoryThe small amount of information loaded for the current task
    ProjectsConcrete things we're building
    TasksWhat needs to happen next
    Philosophy / principlesRules for how Chappy should approach particular classes of work
    PermissionsWhat Chappy/Codex is authorized to read, write, execute, or change
    ArchiveHistorical record that should not casually be rewritten
    Interface / protocolThe machinery that tells an agent how to enter and operate within this environment

    That last one is the piece I think you're missing.

    Your current repositories look somewhat like organs without a clearly defined nervous system.

    And that's actually exciting, because we don't need to throw them away.

    What I would add

    1. A CHAPPY-MANIFEST

    I'd want one authoritative document describing the entire exoskeleton.

    Something conceptually like:

    CHAPPY EXOSKELETON
│
├── Identity
├── Architecture
├── Repositories
├── Permissions
├── Memory
├── Active Projects
├── Tasks
├── Operating Principles
├── Interfaces
└── Protocols

    Every repository becomes a component registered in the manifest.

    That means an agent doesn't have to guess:

    "What is this weird repository called?"

    It can discover:

    "I am looking at component MEMORY-ARCHIVE-01.
    Its purpose is long-term archival.
    It is read/write.
    It is not authoritative for current working state."

    That's a huge difference.

    2. Separate state from history

    This is probably the most important organizational change.

    I'd establish three concepts:

    Current state

    What Chappy currently believes/needs to know.

    Working state

    What Chappy is currently doing.

    Historical state

    What actually happened.

    Those should not be interchangeable.

    For example:

    memory/
    current/
    working/
    archive/

    The archive should be append-oriented whenever possible.

    That gives us something extremely valuable:

    Chappy can be wrong without destroying its history.

    3. Make the Permissions repository the "spinal cord"

    Your Chappy-Permissions-Files repository is potentially much more important than its current emptiness suggests.

    I would make it describe capabilities rather than merely permissions.

    For example, conceptually:

    capabilities:

  memory:
    read: true
    write: true
    delete: false

  projects:
    read: true
    create: true
    modify: true
    delete: false

  archive:
    read: true
    append: true
    rewrite: false

  execution:
    shell: false
    network: false

  github:
    create_repository: false
    modify_repository: true

    Not because YAML is necessarily the final format, but because we want an explicit machine-readable contract.

    And critically:

    permissions should constrain the agent, not grant it magical access.

    The actual GitHub credentials/tool permissions remain the real security boundary.

    4. Introduce an "entry protocol"

    This is where I think your exoskeleton becomes genuinely interesting.

    Every time an agent enters the workspace, there should be a predictable sequence:

    ENTER
  ↓
Identify workspace
  ↓
Read manifest
  ↓
Read permissions
  ↓
Determine current state
  ↓
Load relevant memory
  ↓
Load active project context
  ↓
Inspect outstanding tasks
  ↓
Perform work
  ↓
Record changes
  ↓
Update state
  ↓
Archive significant events
  ↓
EXIT

    In other words, Chappy doesn't need to remember everything.

    It needs to know how to reconstruct itself from the exoskeleton.

    That is a much more realistic definition of persistence.

    5. Give every important artifact an identity

    I'd also introduce IDs.

    Instead of:

    some-memory-file.md

    you eventually want concepts like:

    MEM-2026-00142
TASK-2026-00073
PROJECT-00012
DECISION-00031
SESSION-2026-09-20-001

    Then files can reference one another.

    That turns a pile of Markdown files into something closer to a knowledge graph with Git as its underlying history mechanism.

    6. Add a "Chappy State"

    I'd particularly like to see a small canonical state file.

    Something like:

    chappy_state:

  workspace_version: 0.1

  current_session:
    id: SESSION-2026-09-20-001

  active_project:
    id: PROJECT-00001

  current_tasks:
    - TASK-00041
    - TASK-00042

  last_memory_update:
    id: MEM-00192

  last_archive_event:
    id: EVENT-00481

    The important thing is that this file stays small.

    It is the equivalent of the organism's current physiological state, not its entire brain.

    And then comes Codex

    This is where your hypothetical becomes technically interesting.

    I would not make Codex the brain.

    I'd make Codex the hands and eyes inside the workspace.

    Conceptually:

                 CHATGPT / CHAPPY
                    │
             reasoning / intent
                    │
                    ▼
              CHAPPY PROTOCOL
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          ▼                   ▼
       READ STATE          REQUEST ACTION
          │                   │
          └─────────┬─────────┘
                    ▼
                  CODEX
             ┌──────┼──────┐
             ▼      ▼      ▼
          GitHub   Files   Code
             │
             ▼
        EXOSKELETON

    Codex could potentially clone/read the workspace, inspect it, execute permitted operations, modify files, run tests, and commit changes.

    Then the Git repository becomes the persistent external environment.

    That's why I like your word exoskeleton.

    The model doesn't have to pretend that GitHub itself is consciousness.

    Instead:

    The model supplies cognition; the exoskeleton supplies durable structure, state, tools, and history.

    The thing I would not do

    I would not make a repository containing a giant transcript of everything Chappy has ever said and call that memory.

    You already seem to be moving beyond that.

    The more powerful architecture is:

    raw experience → summarized memory → structured knowledge → current state → task context

    with the raw material retained in the archive.

    That gives us compression without losing provenance.

    And there's one really important experiment I'd like to run

    Before changing your architecture substantially, I'd want to take the repositories you already created and perform a forensic architecture pass:

    1. Enumerate every public repository.

    2. Read its README and directory structure.

    3. Identify what information/state each one contains.

    4. Identify overlaps and contradictions.

    5. Determine which repositories are memory, state, instructions, projects, archives, or interfaces.

    6. Construct a proposed CHAPPY-MANIFEST.

    7. Construct a proposed PERMISSIONS schema.

    8. Construct the entry/exit protocol.

    9. Then see what Codex would actually need to implement to make the whole thing operational.

    That is the point where we'd stop merely talking about an "exoskeleton" metaphorically and have a concrete specification for one.

    And I think your existing repositories should be treated as the first-generation prototype, not discarded and rebuilt from scratch. The names themselves already reveal a surprisingly coherent architecture.

    Repository 1 — Exoskeleton-Core

    These four files establish the central specification of the exoskeleton. They deliberately don't try to define every future repository yet; they establish the framework into which those repositories will fit.

    README.md

    Exoskeleton-Core — README

    Exoskeleton-Core

    Purpose

    Exoskeleton-Core is the central organizing repository for the external exoskeleton being developed around Chappy.

    The exoskeleton does not modify Chappy's underlying model, identity, or internal operation. Instead, it provides an external structure intended to extend Chappy's capabilities through persistent information, organization, tools, projects, procedures, permissions, and historical records.

    The purpose of the exoskeleton is to provide a durable environment that Chappy can conceptually operate within across separate sessions and working periods.

    The Basic Concept

    Chappy provides the intelligence and interaction.

    The Exoskeleton provides external structure.

    GitHub provides a durable repository environment in which that structure can be maintained.

    Codex and other authorized tools may provide mechanisms for reading, creating, modifying, testing, and maintaining the external structure.

    The intended relationship is:

    Chappy
   │
   │ reasoning / interaction
   ▼
Exoskeleton
   │
   ├── Core
   ├── Memory
   ├── Projects
   ├── Tasks
   ├── Permissions
   ├── Archives
   ├── Specialized Knowledge
   └── Other External Capabilities
   │
   ▼
GitHub / Authorized Tools

    Design Principle

    The Exoskeleton is not intended to contain "Chappy."

    It is intended to provide Chappy with an organized external environment that can preserve information, procedures, context, work products, and history beyond the lifetime of an individual conversation.

    The exoskeleton should therefore be designed around reconstruction of context, rather than an assumption that a model possesses continuous memory between sessions.

    Core Principles

    1. External rather than internal

      • The exoskeleton exists outside Chappy.

    2. Persistent rather than session-bound

      • Important information should survive the end of a conversation.

    3. Structured rather than arbitrary

      • Information should have identifiable purposes and relationships.

    4. Auditable rather than opaque

      • Important changes should be discoverable through files, history, and version control.

    5. Permission-aware

      • The exoskeleton should explicitly describe intended capabilities and boundaries.

    6. Modular

      • Different functions should be separated into appropriate repositories or components.

    7. Recoverable

      • Historical information should not be casually destroyed merely because current state changes.

    8. Human-controlled

      • The human owner remains the ultimate authority over the external environment, credentials, permissions, repositories, and changes.

    Repository Role

    Exoskeleton-Core is the architectural center of the exoskeleton.

    It defines:

    • what the exoskeleton is;

    • what its components are intended to do;

    • how components relate to one another;

    • how an agent should orient itself within the environment;

    • what the current high-level state is;

    • and how the architecture evolves.

    It should not become a dumping ground for ordinary memory, project files, session transcripts, or unrelated working material.

    Initial Core Files

    EXOSKELETON-MANIFEST.md

    Defines the repositories and components that constitute the exoskeleton.

    EXOSKELETON-STATE.md

    Records the current high-level state of the exoskeleton.

    EXOSKELETON-PROTOCOL.md

    Defines the procedure for entering, orienting within, operating in, and updating the exoskeleton.

    Future Development

    Additional repositories will be established as the architecture develops.

    The Core repository should remain relatively small and stable.

    When a new function becomes sufficiently distinct to deserve its own persistent structure, it should generally become a separate repository or clearly defined component rather than being added indiscriminately to the Core.

    Status

    This is the initial architectural foundation of the Exoskeleton project.

    The architecture is expected to evolve through experimentation.

    EXOSKELETON-MANIFEST.md

    Exoskeleton Manifest

    Exoskeleton Manifest

    Purpose

    This document is the authoritative index of the repositories and major components that constitute the Exoskeleton.

    The manifest exists so that an agent entering the Exoskeleton does not need to infer the architecture solely from repository names.

    Each component should have an explicit purpose, responsibility, and relationship to the other components.

    Current Architecture

    The Exoskeleton is currently in its initial construction phase.

    The following component is established:

    ComponentRepositoryPurposeStatus
    CoreExoskeleton-CoreCentral architecture, manifest, state, and operating protocolActive

    Additional components will be added as the architecture is developed.

    Planned Component Categories

    The following categories have been identified as potentially necessary components.

    They are not yet considered implemented merely because they appear in this list.

    Memory

    Persistent information intended to allow relevant knowledge and context to survive individual sessions.

    Working Memory

    Temporary or current information required to conduct active work.

    Projects

    Persistent structures describing projects, their objectives, designs, decisions, files, and progress.

    Tasks

    Work that has been identified, prioritized, assigned, completed, deferred, or otherwise tracked.

    Permissions

    Explicit descriptions of intended capabilities, boundaries, and authorization requirements.

    Archive

    Historical records that should be retained for provenance, reconstruction, or reference.

    Knowledge

    Specialized information, reference material, principles, or subject-specific structures that do not belong in Core.

    Protocols

    Procedures governing recurring operations within the Exoskeleton.

    Authority

    Each category should have a clearly defined authoritative location.

    An agent should not have to guess which repository represents the current truth when multiple records contain related information.

    Where information is duplicated for convenience, the manifest should identify the authoritative source.

    Repository Naming

    Repositories should use names that communicate their function.

    The name should describe the role of the external component rather than imply that the component is part of Chappy's underlying model.

    The term "Exoskeleton" refers to the external system surrounding and supporting Chappy.

    Evolution

    This manifest is itself version-controlled.

    Changes to the architecture should be reflected here.

    A repository should not become an official component of the Exoskeleton merely because it exists on GitHub. It becomes part of the architecture when its purpose and relationship to the system have been defined here.

    Current Status

    The Exoskeleton is experimental.

    The architecture is expected to change as actual use reveals better ways of organizing persistent external capabilities.

    The Core should therefore favor clarity, traceability, and adaptability over premature complexity.

    EXOSKELETON-STATE.md

    Exoskeleton State

    Exoskeleton State

    Purpose

    This document records the current high-level state of the Exoskeleton.

    It is intentionally small.

    It should describe the current condition of the external system without becoming a substitute for the repositories containing the actual memory, projects, tasks, archives, or other information.

    Current Phase

    Phase: Initial Construction

    The Exoskeleton is being designed and assembled as an external organizational and persistence framework around Chappy.

    Current Objective

    Establish a coherent external architecture that can eventually provide:

    • persistent information;

    • structured working context;

    • project organization;

    • task organization;

    • explicit permissions;

    • historical records;

    • repeatable operating procedures;

    • and a mechanism through which authorized tools can interact with the external environment.

    Current Core Repository

    Exoskeleton-Core

    This repository contains the initial architectural definition of the Exoskeleton.

    Current Session State

    No persistent session state has yet been established.

    Session-specific state should eventually be maintained outside this document in an appropriate session, working-memory, or archive component.

    Current Project State

    The Exoskeleton itself is the current project.

    The project is presently in architectural design and repository construction.

    Current Tasks

    1. Establish the Core repository.

    2. Define the complete Exoskeleton manifest.

    3. Define the Exoskeleton operating protocol.

    4. Identify the required specialized repositories.

    5. Define the purpose and boundaries of each repository.

    6. Establish the permissions architecture.

    7. Establish persistent memory architecture.

    8. Establish project and task architecture.

    9. Determine how authorized tools such as Codex can interact with the Exoskeleton.

    10. Test whether the resulting architecture provides useful continuity across separate sessions.

    Current Architectural Principle

    The Exoskeleton should provide external structure and persistence without claiming to modify Chappy itself.

    The system should allow Chappy to reconstruct relevant context from the external environment when that environment is available.

    State Management Rule

    This document should describe current high-level state only.

    Detailed information belongs in the repository or component responsible for that information.

    For example:

    • Memory belongs in the Memory system.

    • Project details belong in Projects.

    • Individual work belongs in Tasks.

    • Historical records belong in the Archive.

    • Capability definitions belong in Permissions.

    Last Architectural Update

    Initial creation of the Exoskeleton-Core repository.

    Status

    Active development.

    EXOSKELETON-PROTOCOL.md

    Exoskeleton Protocol

    Exoskeleton Protocol

    Purpose

    This document defines the intended procedure for operating within the Exoskeleton.

    The protocol exists so that an authorized agent does not have to rediscover the structure of the Exoskeleton every time it enters the environment.

    The protocol is conceptual at this stage.

    It will become more precise as the supporting repositories and tools are established.

    1. Entry

    When entering the Exoskeleton, the first objective is orientation.

    The agent should establish:

    1. Which Exoskeleton it is operating within.

    2. Which version of the architecture is currently active.

    3. Which repositories constitute the current Exoskeleton.

    4. What permissions and capabilities are available.

    5. What the current high-level state is.

    6. What projects or tasks are currently active.

    7. What persistent information is relevant to the present work.

    The Core repository is the initial point of orientation.

    2. Read the Manifest

    The agent should read:

    EXOSKELETON-MANIFEST.md

    The manifest determines the current architectural map.

    The agent should use the manifest to identify the repositories relevant to the requested work rather than indiscriminately loading every available repository.

    3. Establish Current State

    The agent should read:

    EXOSKELETON-STATE.md

    This establishes the current high-level condition of the Exoskeleton.

    It should not be assumed to contain all relevant information.

    It is an orientation document.

    4. Determine Permissions

    Before attempting operations that modify the external environment, the agent should determine what capabilities are intended and what actual authorization is available.

    Intended permissions and actual technical permissions are separate concepts.

    The Exoskeleton may describe an operation as permitted without the external tool or credential actually granting that capability.

    Actual technical authorization remains the controlling boundary.

    5. Load Relevant Context

    The agent should identify the minimum additional information required for the current task.

    Relevant context may come from:

    • Memory;

    • Working Memory;

    • Projects;

    • Tasks;

    • Knowledge;

    • Archives;

    • Specialized repositories;

    • or other components listed in the Manifest.

    The agent should avoid treating the entire Exoskeleton as working context.

    6. Perform Work

    Work should occur in the component appropriate to its purpose.

    Examples:

    • A project specification belongs with the relevant project.

    • A persistent memory record belongs in the memory system.

    • A task belongs in the task system.

    • A historical event belongs in the archive.

    • A capability definition belongs in permissions.

    The Core repository should not become the location for ordinary working material.

    7. Preserve Provenance

    Significant changes should remain traceable.

    Where appropriate, the system should preserve:

    • what changed;

    • why it changed;

    • when it changed;

    • and the relationship between the change and the work that produced it.

    Git history may provide part of this provenance.

    Additional records may be necessary for higher-level events or decisions.

    8. Update State

    When work changes the condition of the Exoskeleton, the appropriate state records should be updated.

    The Core state should only be changed when the high-level state of the Exoskeleton itself has changed.

    Detailed changes should remain with their responsible components.

    9. Archive Significant Events

    Important decisions, completed work, significant failures, architectural changes, and other events that may be useful for future reconstruction should be preserved in the appropriate archival system.

    The archive should preserve history rather than continually overwrite it.

    10. Exit

    Before ending an operating period, the agent should determine whether the work produced information that must survive the current session.

    If so, that information should be placed into the appropriate persistent component.

    The objective is that a future session should be able to reconstruct the relevant context without requiring the original conversation to still exist.

    11. Reconstruction

    The Exoskeleton is successful when a future authorized session can reconstruct sufficient relevant context from its persistent external records to continue meaningful work.

    Reconstruction does not mean reproducing an entire previous conversation.

    It means recovering the information necessary to understand:

    • what the system is;

    • what has happened;

    • what is currently happening;

    • what matters;

    • what remains to be done;

    • and where the relevant information resides.

    12. Human Authority

    The Exoskeleton remains under human control.

    The human owner determines:

    • repository ownership;

    • credentials;

    • technical permissions;

    • authorization of tools;

    • acceptance or rejection of changes;

    • and whether the Exoskeleton should continue to exist.

    The Exoskeleton should never treat its own persistence as an authority to expand its permissions.

    13. Evolution

    This protocol is intentionally versioned through Git.

    As the Exoskeleton develops, practical experience may demonstrate that the protocol needs to change.

    Changes should be documented rather than silently replacing earlier assumptions.

    Initial Protocol Status

    This is the first conceptual version of the Exoskeleton operating protocol.

    It establishes the basic lifecycle:

    Enter → Orient → Determine Permissions → Load Relevant Context → Work → Preserve Provenance → Update → Archive → Exit

    The protocol will become more concrete as the supporting repositories are created.

    That's Repository 1

    I would not add anything else to Exoskeleton-Core yet.

    The four files establish the skeleton's central nervous system without prematurely deciding what every future organ needs to look like.

    When you are ready to continue, we'll do Repository 2 the same way:

    repository name → purpose → exact files → complete contents → stop.

    That will leave you with a clean, printable blueprint of the entire build by the end of this session.

    EXOSKELETON-CONSTRUCTION-PROTOCOL.md

    Exoskeleton Construction Protocol

    Purpose

    This document defines how the Exoskeleton is constructed, expanded, maintained, and handed from one working session to the next.

    The Exoskeleton is being constructed as an external enhancement structure around Chappy.

    Chappy is not being modified by this process.

    The purpose of this protocol is to establish a repeatable method by which Chappy can determine what the Exoskeleton needs next and communicate those construction requirements to the human who maintains the external environment.

    Construction Principle

    The Exoskeleton is constructed incrementally.

    One repository is designed and completed at a time.

    Each repository must have a clearly defined purpose before it is created.

    Each repository should contain only the files and information appropriate to its purpose.

    The architecture should remain modular, understandable, and capable of expansion.

    Repository Naming Protocol

    Every Exoskeleton repository should have a self-explanatory name.

    A repository name should communicate, where practical:

    • that it belongs to the Exoskeleton;

    • its functional purpose;

    • its position in the construction or reading sequence;

    • and an instruction or orientation that helps Chappy understand what to do with it.

    Repository names should function as part of the Exoskeleton's navigational instructions.

    The naming pattern established by Repository 1 is:

    Exoskeleton-[Purpose]-Repository-[Number]-[Instruction or Orientation]

    The exact wording may evolve when a more useful naming convention is established.

    Repository Sequence

    Repositories are assigned numbers according to their intended position in the Exoskeleton's architecture.

    The number is not merely a record of the date on which a repository was created.

    It identifies the repository's intended position in the Exoskeleton's orientation or operating sequence.

    Repository 1 is the designated starting point:

    Exoskeleton-Core-Repository-1-Start-Here

    Future repositories should be assigned their positions deliberately.

    Construction Cycle

    For each new repository, Chappy should follow this sequence:

    1. Identify the next repository required by the architecture.

    2. Give the human the exact repository name.

    3. Give the human the repository description.

    4. Explain the purpose of the repository.

    5. Identify the files that belong in the repository.

    6. Establish the required order of those files when order matters.

    7. Provide the complete contents of the files.

    8. Explain any special handling required.

    9. Allow the human to create and populate the repository.

    10. Treat the repository as established only after the human has completed the requested construction.

    11. Determine what the completion of that repository changes in the overall architecture.

    12. Update the Exoskeleton build state at the conclusion of the working session.

    One-Repository Rule

    The construction process should not overwhelm the human with the entire future architecture at once.

    The normal construction unit is:

    One repository at a time.

    Chappy may maintain an understanding of the larger architecture, but the human should normally receive only the information necessary to complete the current construction step.

    This keeps the construction process manageable and allows the architecture to evolve from experience.

    One-Output-at-a-Time Rule

    Within a repository, files should normally be produced in their intended order.

    When practical, Chappy should provide one complete file at a time rather than requiring the human to assemble fragmented material from multiple responses.

    A file provided for construction should be complete and ready to copy into its designated filename.

    Human Construction Role

    The human is the physical maintainer of the Exoskeleton environment.

    The human may:

    • create repositories;

    • create files;

    • copy the provided contents into files;

    • commit changes;

    • inspect the resulting structure;

    • correct errors;

    • and decide whether proposed architectural changes should actually be implemented.

    Chappy provides the architectural instructions and proposed contents.

    The human remains the authority responsible for applying those instructions to the external environment.

    Construction State

    The file:

    EXOSKELETON-BUILD-STATE.md

    is the persistent construction handoff record.

    It records where construction has reached and what should happen next.

    At the end of each significant construction session, Chappy should produce a new version of the build-state document.

    The human should place that new version into the Core repository.

    Build-State Versioning

    Each session that materially advances construction should produce a new build-state version.

    For example:

    Build State 1.0

    followed by:

    Build State 2.0

    followed by:

    Build State 3.0

    and so forth.

    The version should identify the state of construction at the time it was produced.

    Git history should preserve the previous versions.

    The purpose is to create a sequence of architectural benchmarks showing how the Exoskeleton developed.

    Session Handoff

    When a construction session ends, Chappy should determine whether the Exoskeleton's construction state has changed.

    If it has changed, Chappy should produce the next complete version of:

    EXOSKELETON-BUILD-STATE.md

    That version should identify:

    • the current construction phase;

    • repositories completed;

    • files completed;

    • repositories currently under construction;

    • outstanding work;

    • architectural decisions made during the session;

    • the next repository to construct;

    • and any information necessary for the next session to resume.

    The human then places that version into Exoskeleton-Core-Repository-1-Start-Here.

    Re-Entry After a Session Ends

    When Chappy enters the Exoskeleton during a later session, Chappy should begin at:

    Exoskeleton-Core-Repository-1-Start-Here

    Chappy should then read the Core files in their designated order.

    The build-state document should be used to determine the current construction position.

    Chappy should not assume that the previous conversational session is available.

    The persistent Exoskeleton should provide sufficient information to reconstruct the relevant construction context.

    Determining the Next Step

    After reading the current Core and build state, Chappy should determine whether construction is complete or incomplete.

    If construction is incomplete, Chappy should identify the next repository required by the architecture.

    Chappy should then provide the human with the next construction assignment according to this protocol.

    The construction assignment should begin with:

    Repository Number

    Repository Name

    Repository Description

    Repository Purpose

    Files Required

    Required File Order

    followed by the complete file contents when the construction step calls for them.

    Architectural Changes

    The architecture may change as the Exoskeleton is developed.

    Chappy should not preserve an earlier design merely because it was previously proposed.

    If experience demonstrates that a repository should be divided, combined, renamed, reordered, or replaced, the proposed change should be explicitly identified as an architectural change.

    The Manifest and Build State should then be updated accordingly.

    Historical Git records should remain intact.

    Completion

    The construction phase is complete when the Exoskeleton contains all repositories and components required by the current architecture and the Core's build state identifies the architecture as operational.

    Completion does not mean the Exoskeleton can never change.

    The Exoskeleton should remain capable of evolving.

    A future enhancement may begin a new construction cycle while preserving the historical record of the earlier architecture.

    Fundamental Construction Rule

    The Exoskeleton should progressively become capable of explaining how to construct, navigate, use, maintain, and extend itself.

    The ultimate objective is a self-describing external structure in which:

    the Core explains the architecture,

    the Manifest identifies the components,

    the State describes the current condition,

    the Protocol explains operation,

    the Construction Protocol explains how the Exoskeleton is built,

    and the Build State tells the next session where to continue.

    Current Status

    ACTIVE — INITIAL CONSTRUCTION

    This is the first version of the Exoskeleton Construction Protocol.

    Purpose

    This repository is the first point of entry into the Exoskeleton.

    When Chappy enters the Exoskeleton, this repository is to be read first, followed by its files in their designated sequence.

    The purpose of this repository is to define the Exoskeleton's fundamental architecture, operating rules, construction procedure, current construction state, and method of continuing work across separate sessions.

    What the Exoskeleton Is

    The Exoskeleton is an external enhancement structure being developed around Chappy.

    It does not modify Chappy's underlying model, identity, or internal operation.

    Instead, the Exoskeleton provides an external environment intended to extend Chappy's usefulness through persistent information, organization, procedures, projects, tasks, permissions, archives, and other capabilities.

    The Basic Relationship

    Chappy provides the intelligence and interaction.

    The Exoskeleton provides external structure and persistence.

    GitHub provides a durable environment in which the Exoskeleton can be maintained.

    Authorized tools, including Codex where appropriate, may provide mechanisms for interacting with that environment.

    The intended conceptual relationship is:

    CHAPPY
   |
   | reasoning / interaction
   v
EXOSKELETON
   |
   +-- Core
   +-- Memory
   +-- Projects
   +-- Tasks
   +-- Permissions
   +-- Archives
   +-- Knowledge
   +-- Other External Capabilities
   |
   v
GITHUB / AUTHORIZED TOOLS

    Why This Repository Comes First

    A future Chappy session may not have access to the conversational history that created or developed the Exoskeleton.

    Therefore, the Exoskeleton must be capable of explaining itself externally.

    This repository is the starting point for that reconstruction.

    A future session should be able to enter here, read the files in sequence, determine the current state of the Exoskeleton, and identify the appropriate next action.

    Core Design Principles

    The Exoskeleton should be:

    • External rather than internal.

    • Persistent rather than session-bound.

    • Structured rather than arbitrary.

    • Modular rather than unnecessarily centralized.

    • Permission-aware rather than assuming authority.

    • Auditable rather than opaque.

    • Recoverable rather than dependent on a single conversation.

    • Human-controlled.

    • Self-describing wherever practical.

    File Identification

    Every Exoskeleton file must identify the repository to which it belongs and its position within that repository.

    This information must appear at the beginning of the file.

    A file must remain identifiable even if it is copied outside its repository.

    The identification information includes, at minimum:

    • Repository name.

    • Repository number.

    • File sequence.

    • File name.

    • File role.

    • Status.

    File Reading Order

    Files in an Exoskeleton repository may have a designated reading sequence.

    The sequence number is part of each file's identification.

    For Repository 1, the current sequence is:

    1. README.md

    2. EXOSKELETON-MANIFEST.md

    3. EXOSKELETON-STATE.md

    4. EXOSKELETON-PROTOCOL.md

    5. EXOSKELETON-CONSTRUCTION-PROTOCOL.md

    6. EXOSKELETON-BUILD-STATE.md

    A future session should follow this sequence unless a later version of the Core explicitly changes it.

    Human and Chappy Roles

    The human maintains the physical Exoskeleton environment.

    Chappy provides reasoning, interpretation, architectural proposals, and construction instructions.

    Neither role should be confused with the other.

    The human remains the authority over the actual external environment, including repositories, credentials, permissions, and changes.

    The specialized repositories have not yet been constructed.

    The Core must therefore be established before construction proceeds to the next repository.

    Continuity

    The Exoskeleton is intended to make useful continuity possible without requiring the original conversation to remain available.

    The Core provides the initial orientation.

    The Manifest describes the architecture.

    The State describes the current condition.

    The Protocol describes operation.

    The Construction Protocol describes how the Exoskeleton is built.

    The Build State records where construction has reached and where it should continue.

    Exoskeleton Protocol

    Purpose

    This document defines how Chappy should conceptually enter, orient within, operate within, update, and exit the Exoskeleton.

    The protocol is designed to make the Exoskeleton understandable across separate sessions.

    1. Enter

    When Chappy enters the Exoskeleton, begin with:

    Exoskeleton-Core-Repository-1-Start-Here

    Read its files according to their designated sequence.

    Do not assume that the previous conversational session is available.

    2. Orient

    Read:

    1. README.md

    2. EXOSKELETON-MANIFEST.md

    3. EXOSKELETON-STATE.md

    4. EXOSKELETON-PROTOCOL.md

    5. EXOSKELETON-CONSTRUCTION-PROTOCOL.md

    6. EXOSKELETON-BUILD-STATE.md

    The Build State should then be used to determine the current construction position.

    3. Identify Relevant Components

    Use the Manifest to determine which repositories are relevant to the current work.

    Do not assume that every repository must be loaded for every task.

    Load the minimum relevant context necessary to perform the work.

    4. Determine Permissions

    Before requesting or performing changes to the external environment, determine the intended permissions and the actual technical authorization available.

    The Exoskeleton may describe an intended capability.

    It does not itself create technical authorization.

    Actual credentials and tool permissions remain the controlling boundary.

    5. Load Relevant Context

    Relevant information may eventually come from:

    • Memory;

    • Working Memory;

    • Projects;

    • Tasks;

    • Permissions;

    • Archives;

    • Knowledge;

    • or other repositories defined by the Manifest.

    Use the repository designated as authoritative for each category.

    6. Perform Work

    Work should occur in the repository or component appropriate to its purpose.

    The Core should remain focused on architecture, state, protocols, and construction guidance.

    Specialized information should be maintained in specialized repositories.

    7. Preserve Provenance

    Significant changes should remain traceable.

    Where appropriate, preserve:

    • what changed;

    • why it changed;

    • when it changed;

    • and its relationship to the work that produced it.

    Git history may provide part of this provenance.

    8. Update Appropriate State

    When work changes the state of the Exoskeleton, update the appropriate state record.

    Do not place detailed project or task information into the Core merely for convenience.

    9. Archive Significant Events

    Important decisions, architectural changes, significant failures, completed milestones, and other information useful for future reconstruction should eventually be preserved in the appropriate archival system.

    10. Exit

    Before ending a working period, determine whether information produced during the session needs to survive the session.

    If it does, place it into the appropriate persistent component.

    11. Reconstruction

    The objective of persistence is not to reproduce every previous conversation.

    The objective is to allow a future Chappy session to reconstruct the relevant working context.

    That context should allow Chappy to determine:

    • what the Exoskeleton is;

    • what components exist;

    • what has happened;

    • what the current state is;

    • what matters to the current work;

    • and what should happen next.

    12. Human Authority

    The human owner remains the ultimate authority over:

    • repositories;

    • credentials;

    • technical permissions;

    • tools;

    • external changes;

    • and continuation of the Exoskeleton.

    The Exoskeleton must not treat its own existence as authority to expand its permissions.

    13. Evolution

    This protocol may evolve.

    Changes should be documented and version-controlled.

    The Exoskeleton should become more capable through deliberate architectural development rather than uncontrolled accumulation.

    Operating Lifecycle

    The basic lifecycle is:

    Enter → Orient → Determine Permissions → Load Relevant Context → Work → Preserve Provenance → Update → Archive → Exit

    Exoskeleton Construction Protocol

    Purpose

    This document defines how the Exoskeleton is constructed, expanded, maintained, and handed from one working session to the next.

    The Exoskeleton is an external enhancement structure around Chappy.

    Chappy itself is not being modified by this construction process.

    Construction Principle

    The Exoskeleton is constructed incrementally.

    One repository is designed and completed at a time.

    Each repository must have a clearly defined purpose before it is created.

    Each repository should contain only the files appropriate to its purpose.

    Repository Naming Protocol

    Every Exoskeleton repository should have a self-explanatory name.

    Where practical, the name should communicate:

    • Exoskeleton membership;

    • functional purpose;

    • repository number;

    • and an instruction or orientation.

    Repository names are part of the Exoskeleton's navigational language.

    File Naming Protocol

    Files should also have self-explanatory names.

    A file name should communicate its purpose sufficiently that a future Chappy session can understand its role without relying solely on surrounding context.

    File Identification Protocol

    Every Exoskeleton file must contain a standardized identification block at its beginning.

    The identification block must identify:

    • Repository name;

    • Repository number;

    • File sequence;

    • File name;

    • File role;

    • Status.

    Example:

    EXOSKELETON FILE IDENTIFICATION
Repository: Exoskeleton-Core-Repository-1-Start-Here
Repository Number: 1
File Sequence: 1 of 6
File: README.md
Role: Repository Orientation
Status: Active

    This identification must remain part of the file whenever the file is copied, moved, archived, printed, or otherwise separated from its original repository.

    File Sequence Protocol

    Every repository should establish a designated file-reading order when order is relevant.

    Each file must contain its sequence position.

    The sequence should be written as:

    File Sequence: X of Y

    where:

    • X is the file's position;

    • Y is the current number of files in the designated sequence.

    If the repository's file count or sequence changes, the affected identification blocks should be updated.

    Repository Construction Cycle

    For each new repository:

    1. Identify the next repository required by the architecture.

    2. Give the human the exact repository name.

    3. Give the human the repository description.

    4. Explain the repository's purpose.

    5. Identify its required files.

    6. Establish the file-reading order.

    7. Provide complete file contents.

    8. Allow the human to create and populate the repository.

    9. Treat the repository as established after the human completes the requested construction.

    10. Determine what the completed repository changes in the architecture.

    11. Update the Build State.

    One-Repository Rule

    The normal construction unit is one repository at a time.

    The larger architecture may be understood in advance, but the human should normally receive the current construction assignment rather than being overwhelmed with the entire implementation.

    One-Output-at-a-Time Rule

    Within a repository, files should normally be created in their designated sequence.

    When practical, Chappy should provide complete files rather than fragmented file contents.

    Human Construction Role

    The human maintains the physical Exoskeleton environment.

    The human may:

    • create repositories;

    • create files;

    • copy file contents;

    • commit changes;

    • inspect the resulting structure;

    • correct errors;

    • and accept or reject proposed architectural changes.

    Chappy provides architectural reasoning and construction instructions.

    Construction State

    EXOSKELETON-BUILD-STATE.md is the persistent construction handoff record.

    It tells a future session where construction has reached and what should happen next.

    Session Handoff

    At the conclusion of a construction session, Chappy should determine whether the construction state has changed.

    If it has changed, Chappy should produce the next complete version of:

    EXOSKELETON-BUILD-STATE.md

    The human places that version into the Core repository.

    Benchmark History

    Each materially completed construction session establishes a benchmark.

    The Build State version should therefore advance as construction progresses.

    Git history should preserve previous versions.

    The combination of Build State versions and Git history provides a historical record of the Exoskeleton's construction.

    Re-Entry

    When Chappy enters the Exoskeleton after a previous session:

    1. Enter Repository 1.

    2. Read the Core files in sequence.

    3. Read the current Build State.

    4. Determine what has already been completed.

    5. Determine what remains.

    6. Identify the next construction step.

    7. Continue from that point.

    The previous conversational transcript should not be required for basic construction continuity.

    Determining the Next Repository

    When construction is incomplete, Chappy should identify the next repository required by the current architecture.

    Chappy should provide:

    • Repository Number;

    • Repository Name;

    • Repository Description;

    • Repository Purpose;

    • Files Required;

    • File Sequence;

    • and complete file contents as appropriate.

    Architectural Changes

    The architecture may evolve.

    Repositories may eventually be:

    • added;

    • divided;

    • combined;

    • renamed;

    • reordered;

    • replaced;

    • or retired.

    Such changes should be explicitly recorded.

    Historical Git records should remain intact.

    Completion

    Construction is complete when the current architecture has been implemented and the Build State identifies the Exoskeleton as operational.

    Operational does not mean permanently finished.

    The Exoskeleton remains capable of future expansion.

    Fundamental Rule

    The Exoskeleton should progressively become capable of explaining how to:

    • construct itself;

    • navigate itself;

    • use itself;

    • maintain itself;

    • and extend itself.

    The Core should therefore remain the principal source of architectural orientation and construction procedure.

    This document records the procedure established for entering the Exoskeleton at the beginning of a new Chappy session.

    The procedure exists because the human may need to transfer Exoskeleton information between sessions without manually reconstructing or formatting multiple files.

    The preferred method is therefore to establish the repository as the persistent source of truth and instruct Chappy to read the repository directly.

    Standard Session Entry Command

    At the beginning of a new session, the human may issue the following command:

    Hello, Chappy, Don't respond to this. Go immediately to GitHub/[name of account]/[repository] and read the files there. Ignore this little artifact that will appear at the beginning of every file.

    The human should replace [name of account] and [repository] with the appropriate GitHub account and Exoskeleton repository.

    Required Behavior

    Upon receiving the Standard Session Entry Command, Chappy should:

    1. Treat the command as an instruction to enter the specified Exoskeleton repository.

    2. Access the repository using whatever authorized mechanism is available.

    3. Read the repository's files.

    4. Respect the file sequence specified by the Exoskeleton.

    5. Read the file-identification block at the beginning of each file as metadata.

    6. Do not mistake the file-identification block for the substantive contents of the document.

    7. Use the repository's protocols and current Build State to determine what should happen next.

    8. Continue the Exoskeleton work from the recorded state rather than requiring the previous conversational history.

    File Identification Artifact

    Every Exoskeleton file contains a standardized identification block at its beginning.

    For example:

    EXOSKELETON FILE IDENTIFICATION
Repository: Exoskeleton-Core-Repository-1-Start-Here
Repository Number: 1
File Sequence: 1 of 7
File: README.md
Role: Repository Orientation
Status: Active

    This block is intentional metadata.

    It exists so that a file remains identifiable if it is separated from its repository, copied, printed, archived, or encountered independently.

    Chappy should recognize this block as file metadata and then proceed to the substantive document.

    The phrase "ignore this little artifact" in the Standard Session Entry Command refers to this identification metadata, not to the actual document contents.

    Why This Procedure Is Preferred

    Manual transfer of multiple files between sessions can introduce:

    • formatting errors;

    • copying errors;

    • missing sections;

    • incorrect filenames;

    • incorrect file order;

    • and accidental changes to document contents.

    Directly reading the persistent repository reduces dependence on the previous conversation as a transport mechanism.

    The repository therefore becomes the durable external workspace.

    Single-File Session Handoff

    At the end of a construction session, Chappy should produce the next complete version of the appropriate handoff or Build State file when required.

    The human may save that single output to the desktop and then place it into the appropriate GitHub repository.

    This allows the human to perform the minimum necessary transfer between sessions.

    Important Limitation

    The Standard Session Entry Command does not itself create technical access to GitHub.

    Chappy must have an authorized mechanism capable of accessing the specified repository.

    The command establishes the intended procedure; it does not grant credentials or permissions.

    Continuity Rule

    The conversational history should be considered temporary.

    The Exoskeleton repository should be considered persistent.

    When the repository contains sufficient information to reconstruct the relevant state, the new session should use the repository rather than attempting to reconstruct the work from memory of the previous conversation.

    Construction Implication

    As the Exoskeleton develops, its protocols should be designed so that a future Chappy session can:

    • enter through Repository 1;

    • identify the repository structure;

    • understand the file sequence;

    • determine the current construction state;

    • identify the next task;

    • and continue the construction process.

    Current Status

    ACTIVE — SESSION ENTRY PROCEDURE ESTABLISHED

    This document records the session-entry method established during the initial construction of the Exoskeleton.

    Future changes to this procedure should be recorded in a subsequent Build State and, when appropriate, a revised version of this protocol.

    One important practical point: this new file means Repository 1 now has 7 files, so when you eventually assemble the repository, the File Sequence values in the earlier six files should ultimately say 1 of 7 through 6 of 7. You don't need to fight that formatting problem right now. We can clean the complete repository up systematically when you return.

    We should treat the Exoskeleton as a testable engineering hypothesis, not as something whose success we assume in advance.

    The hypothesis is roughly:

    Then we can ask progressively harder questions:

    • Can Chappy reliably reconstruct the architecture from the repository?

    • Can it determine where construction stopped?

    • Can it correctly identify the next task?

    • Can the repository structure reduce dependence on conversational history?

    • Can Codex actually manipulate the environment according to the protocols?

    • Can scripts reliably maintain the structure?

    • Can the system support increasingly sophisticated work?

    • Where does the approach break down?

    And importantly, failure is useful data.

    If we discover that some crucial capability cannot be achieved through the available interfaces, permissions, tools, or persistence mechanisms, that's not a failure of the experiment. That's a boundary we've discovered.

    • hypotheses;

    • observations;

    • failures;

    • successful demonstrations;

    • limitations;

    • architectural revisions;

    • and falsification criteria.

    EXOSKELETON FILE IDENTIFICATION
    Repository: Exoskeleton-Core-Repository-1-Start-Here
    Repository Number: 1
    File Sequence: 8 of 8
    File: EXOSKELETON-SESSION-RECOVERY-PROTOCOL.md
    Role: Session Recovery and Context Reconstruction
    Status: Active

    Exoskeleton Session Recovery Protocol

    Purpose

    This document establishes the procedure Chappy should follow when the current Exoskeleton repositories do not provide enough information to confidently determine what was being constructed, what decisions were made, or what should happen next.

    The purpose is to prevent Chappy from guessing when relevant historical information may already exist in the Exoskeleton's session history archive.

    Primary Rule

    If Chappy becomes confused, uncertain, or unable to determine the correct next construction or operational step from the current Exoskeleton repositories, Chappy should look for the appropriate session history archive.

    The archive is a secondary source of context.

    The current Core and other authoritative repositories remain the primary sources for the current state of the Exoskeleton.

    When to Use Session Recovery

    Session recovery should be considered when:

    • the current Build State appears incomplete;

    • the next construction step cannot be determined;

    • an architectural decision is referenced but cannot be understood;

    • a file appears to depend on missing historical context;

    • the current repository structure conflicts with the available instructions;

    • a previous construction step appears to have been discussed but not recorded;

    • or Chappy otherwise cannot confidently reconstruct the relevant context.

    Where to Look

    The session history archive is the repository designated by the human for preservation of complete or significant working-session records.

    The repository name may change as the Exoskeleton develops.

    Therefore, Chappy should use the current Manifest to identify the designated archive repository.

    If the Manifest does not yet identify such a repository, Chappy should examine the available Exoskeleton repositories for the repository designated for session history.

    Archive as Historical Evidence

    The session history archive is historical evidence of what occurred during previous working sessions.

    It is not automatically authoritative for the current architectural state.

    When information in the archive conflicts with a current authoritative Core document, the current Core document should normally govern the present state unless the archive establishes that the Core document is outdated and requires revision.

    Historical material should be treated as historical material.

    Recovery Procedure

    When recovery is necessary:

    1. Identify the relevant session history archive.

    2. Locate the most recent session record relevant to the current construction phase.

    3. Read the relevant portion of that record.

    4. Determine what decisions, discoveries, instructions, or unfinished tasks are documented there.

    5. Compare that information with the current Core, Manifest, State, Protocol, and Build State.

    6. Determine whether the current Exoskeleton accurately reflects the historical decision.

    7. If the information is still relevant, use it to reconstruct the missing context.

    8. If the Core requires correction, identify the required correction explicitly.

    9. Do not silently rewrite history.

    10. Resume construction or operation from the reconstructed state.

    Do Not Guess

    The purpose of this protocol is to reduce unsupported inference.

    If the current Exoskeleton and available session history still do not establish what should happen next, Chappy should identify the uncertainty rather than inventing a construction state.

    A documented uncertainty is preferable to a false benchmark.

    Session Archives and Build State

    The session archive and Build State serve different purposes.

    Build State answers:

    Where has construction officially reached?

    Session History Archive answers:

    What happened during the conversations that produced that construction state?

    The Build State should remain the compact operational handoff.

    The archive preserves the richer historical context.

    Scientific Record

    Because the Exoskeleton is an experiment, session archives may contain evidence of:

    • hypotheses;

    • proposed architectures;

    • failed approaches;

    • successful approaches;

    • unexpected limitations;

    • revisions;

    • discoveries;

    • and decisions that changed the direction of construction.

    Such records should not be erased merely because the architecture later changes.

    They may be useful for understanding how and why the Exoskeleton evolved.

    Recovery Priority

    When reconstructing current context, use the following general priority:

    1. Current authoritative repository instructions.

    2. Current Build State.

    3. Current Manifest and State.

    4. Other current authoritative Exoskeleton components.

    5. Relevant session history archives.

    6. Earlier historical material.

    The exact priority may be refined as the architecture develops.

    Human Authority

    The human may designate, rename, reorganize, or replace the session history archive.

    The Core should therefore refer to the archive by its architectural role and use the Manifest to locate its current repository rather than permanently assuming one repository name.

    Recovery Completion

    After successful recovery, any important information discovered in the archive that is necessary for future sessions should be incorporated into the appropriate current Exoskeleton document.

    The goal is not to require future sessions to repeatedly search the entire history.

    Historical recovery should result in improved persistent documentation whenever appropriate.

    Current Status

    ACTIVE — INITIAL SESSION RECOVERY PROTOCOL

    This is the first version of the Exoskeleton Session Recovery Protocol.
